query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Intermediate-temperature thermal aging of an as-cast, single‐phase AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy promotes the nucleation and growth of brittle precipitates (particularly along grain or phase boundaries) that serve as stress concentrators, thereby reducing toughness and favoring brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase solid solution state of the AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to intermediate-temperature thermal aging representative of service conditions.
generation.conditions: Aging at temperatures that are high enough to activate precipitation but below those that would cause full recrystallization or complete phase transformation, under controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Brittle precipitates forming at grain or phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging enables the diffusion of solute atoms, leading to the formation and growth of secondary brittle phases at interfaces. These precipitates weaken the coherence of the boundaries and act as sites for crack initiation and propagation under applied mechanical loads, thus reducing overall toughness and increasing brittleness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged specimens will exhibit reduced fracture toughness and ductility, with microstructural analysis showing discrete precipitate formation along grain or phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: The pristine as-cast single-phase solid solution exhibiting higher toughness and ductility under mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under service conditions where the alloy experiences intermediate temperatures in combination with mechanical stresses, typical of demanding engineering environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise precipitate morphology, their distribution kinetics, and the quantitative extent of toughness reduction remain uncertain without further targeted experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi alloy specimens: one in the as-cast state and one subjected to intermediate-temperature thermal aging. Conduct standardized fracture toughness tests (e.g., Charpy impact or single-edge notch bending) and perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM, TEM, or EBSD) to quantify precipitate formation at grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness values (e.g., K_IC or Charpy impact energy)
Microstructural characterization of precipitate size, distribution, and location
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged specimens do not show a statistically significant decrease in fracture toughness or ductility compared to the as-cast specimens, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of precipitates along grain or phase boundaries, then the hypothesis that intermediate-temperature thermal aging causes embrittlement via precipitate-induced crack initiation is falsified.
